opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Q, K, and V are often explained with a database analogy: the query is what you're looking for, the keys are the labels you match against, and the values are the content you retrieve. That's a reasonable starting point, but I think it's a little too neat. It makes attention sound like exact lookup, when really it's a soft, learned weighting over everything in the context.

I find it more useful to look at the math. Each token's representation gets projected three different ways. The query and key projections exist to compute a similarity score. You take the dot product of one token's query with every other token's key, then softmax that into a distribution. So Q and K together define *who should pay attention to whom*. The value projection then defines *what actually gets passed along* once that decision is made.

The interesting part is why you separate them at all. If you used the raw embedding for everything, the notion of "relevant to me" would be tied to "what I am," and those are different things. A pronoun might want to find a noun, but what it needs to carry back isn't "nounness," it's the specific semantic content of that noun. Splitting Q and K from V decouples matching from content. Splitting Q from K makes the relationship asymmetric: how A attends to B doesn't have to equal how B attends to A, which matters a lot in language.

Another way I think about it: Q times K transposed is effectively a bilinear form, a learned metric over the representation space. Each head learns its own notion of similarity. One head might track syntactic dependencies, another positional proximity, another coreference. V, together with the output projection, decides how that gathered information is written back into the residual stream.

This is also why things like positional encoding are so tied to Q and K specifically. With rotary embeddings, for example, you rotate Q and K so that their inner product depends only on relative position. You don't touch V, because position should influence *where you look*, not necessarily *what you bring back*. Seeing that design choice made the roles click for me: Q and K are the addressing mechanism, and V is the payload.

So my one-sentence version would be this: Q and K jointly build a context-dependent, learnable routing pattern, and V is the information that flows along those routes.

r001.rationale: The response says the query represents what a token is looking for.

r002.rationale: It describes keys as labels other tokens match against and says each query is compared with every other token’s key.

r003.rationale: It explains that the query-key dot product produces a similarity score between tokens.

r004.rationale: It describes values as the content passed along when a token is attended to.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that attention is a soft lookup. You have a bunch of positions in a sequence, and each one wants to pull in information from the others. Q, K, and V are just the three roles in that lookup.

The query is what a position is asking for. It's a vector that says, roughly, "here's the kind of information I need right now." The key is what each position advertises about itself: "here's what I have to offer." You compare the query against every key with a dot product, and that gives you a relevance score for each position. Softmax turns those scores into weights that sum to one. Then the value is the actual content you pull out. You take a weighted average of all the values, using those attention weights, and that becomes the new representation for the querying position.

What I think people sometimes miss is why you need three separate projections instead of one or two. If keys and values were the same vector, then what makes a position worth attending to would be forced to be the same as what it contributes once attended to. Those are different jobs. A token might be very good at signaling "I'm the verb you're looking for" while the useful content to carry forward is something else entirely, like its tense or its argument structure. Splitting K from V lets the model decouple addressing from content. And splitting Q from K means the matching doesn't have to be symmetric. "I'm a pronoun looking for my antecedent" and "I'm a noun that could be an antecedent" are different signals, and asymmetric projections let them meet in a shared space without having to look alike.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that all three come from the same input through learned linear maps. So the model isn't given a notion of what's relevant. It learns to carve the residual stream into "what I'm looking for," "what I can be found by," and "what I pass along." Multi-head attention just does that carving several times in parallel with different projections, so one head can track syntax while another tracks coreference or position.

So if I had to compress it: Q asks, K answers "is this me," and V is what you actually receive. Attention is routing, and the three matrices are how the model learns the routing rules from data.

r001.rationale: It says the query represents what a position is asking for and the information it needs.

r002.rationale: It describes each key as what a position advertises so other queries can find or match it.

r003.rationale: It says the query is compared with every key by dot product to produce relevance scores.

r004.rationale: It explains that values are the actual content pulled from attended positions and combined by weighted average.

astra-6.text:
I think of Q, K, and V as three roles: what I’m looking for, how I can be found, and what information I can provide.

Q is the query. At a particular token position, it represents what information that token is looking for. K is the key: each token offers a key that the query can match against. The similarity between a query and the keys determines the attention weights. V is the value—the information we actually combine using those weights.

In standard scaled dot-product attention, we compute QK transpose, divide by the square root of the key dimension, apply softmax, and then multiply by V. So Q and K determine where to look, while V determines what gets gathered.

In self-attention, Q, K, and V are learned projections of the same input sequence. In cross-attention, the queries come from one sequence, while the keys and values come from another. And with multiple heads, the model can learn several different ways of matching and gathering information at once.

r001.rationale: It says Q represents what information a token is looking for.

r002.rationale: It says each token offers a key that a query can match against, describing how other tokens can find it.

r003.rationale: It says query-key similarity determines attention weights, identifying the QK comparison as the basis for connection strength.

r004.rationale: It describes V as the information combined using the attention weights.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of Q, K, and V as three roles: what I’m looking for, what each item can be matched on, and what information each item carries.

For each token, we take its representation and apply three learned projections to produce a query, a key, and a value. The query is compared with the available keys. In standard scaled dot-product attention, those similarity scores are divided by the square root of the key dimension and passed through a softmax to get attention weights. The output is then a weighted sum of the values.

So Q and K determine where to attend, while V determines what information gets combined. In self-attention, all three come from the same sequence, but their different projections let them serve different purposes. In cross-attention, queries come from one sequence and keys and values come from another.

r001.rationale: Q is described as what a token is looking for.

r002.rationale: K is what each item can be matched on; other tokens’ queries compare against available keys.

r003.rationale: The response says query-key similarity scores determine where to attend, expressing the strength of the match between tokens.

r004.rationale: V is the information each item carries and contributes to the weighted sum.
